topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Linear Algebra or advanced High School students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as an Action
sections.content: Briefly recap that a matrix doesn't just hold numbers; it is a function that transforms space. Show a 2D grid where a matrix A moves the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat to new locations. Establish that A(v) is the 'landing spot' of vector v after transformation A.
sections.example: Visual: A 2D coordinate grid with a 'Space-Cat' character sitting at (1,1). When matrix A is applied, the grid warps, and the Space-Cat is sheared to the right.

sections.title: The Sequence: Two Transformations
sections.content: Introduce the concept of applying two transformations in a row. First, transform the space with Matrix A, then take that result and transform it again with Matrix B. This is the 'Composition' of functions.
sections.example: Visual: Our Space-Cat is first rotated 90 degrees by Matrix A (Step 1). Then, the already-rotated Space-Cat is stretched vertically by Matrix B (Step 2).

sections.title: Defining the 'Shortcut' Matrix
sections.content: Explain that we want a single matrix, let's call it C, that performs both steps in one jump. Mathematically, B(A(v)) = (BA)v. This 'Product Matrix' BA represents the total effect of A followed by B.
sections.example: Visual: A side-by-side comparison. On the left, the two-step process (Rotate then Stretch). On the right, a single 'Combined Matrix' C that teleports the Space-Cat from its original position directly to its final rotated-and-stretched position.

sections.title: The Right-to-Left Rule
sections.content: Address the potential confusion of notation: In the expression BA, the transformation A (on the right) happens FIRST. This is because the vector v is closest to A. Emphasize that matrix multiplication order follows the order of function nesting.
sections.example: Animation: A mechanical arm with two slots for 'Action Chips'. If you slide Chip A in first and then Chip B, the math reads B * A. Show the 'Action' flowing from the vector on the right, through A, then through B.

sections.title: Why Order Matters (Non-Commutativity)
sections.content: Visually demonstrate that AB is not the same as BA. Changing the order of composition usually leads to a completely different result, which is why matrix multiplication is not commutative.
sections.example: Visual: Compare (1) Rotating the Space-Cat then moving it 5 units right vs. (2) Moving it 5 units right then rotating it around the origin. The final positions are different, proving BA ≠ AB.

sections.title: Summary: Matrix Multiplication is Combining Actions
sections.content: Conclude that matrix multiplication is not just a tedious calculation of rows and columns; it is the mathematical way to 'glue' linear transformations together.
sections.example: Visual: A 'Macro' view of a complex animation (like a character walking) being broken down into a series of matrices (Leg rotation * Knee bend * Hip tilt) multiplied together to create one fluid motion.
